whale.e: From Middle English whal, whale, from Old English hwæl (“whale”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwal, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz (“whale”) (compare German Wal, Swedish val, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål hval, Norwegian Nynorsk kval; compare also Dutch walvis, West Frisian walfisk.
whale.g: Any large cetacean, usually with the exclusion of dolphins and porpoises.

whale.e: Uncertain. Perhaps a variant of wale influenced by whack, whap, etc.
whale.g: To thrash, to flog, to beat vigorously or soundly.

what.e: From Middle English what, from Old English hwæt (“what”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat (“what”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷód (“what”), neuter form of *kʷós (“who”).
what.g: Which, especially which of an open-ended set of possibilities.

whatever.e: From Middle English whatever. By surface analysis, what + -ever.
whatever.g: A thing or person whose actual name is unknown or forgotten.

whatsoever.e: From Middle English whatsoever. By surface analysis, what + so + -ever.

wheat.e: From Middle English whete, from Old English hwǣte, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaitī, from Proto-Germanic *hwaitijaz (compare West Frisian weet, Dutch weit, Low German Weten, German Weizen, Danish hvede, Swedish vete, Norwegian Bokmål hvete, Norwegian Nynorsk kveite, Faroese and Icelandic hveiti), from *hwītaz (“white”).
wheat.g: Any of the several cereal grains, of the genus Triticum, that yields flour as used in bakery.

wheaten.e: From Middle English wheten, from Old English hwǣten (“wheaten”); equivalent to wheat + -en.
wheaten.g: Of, pertaining to, or made from wheat.

wheel.e: From Middle English whel, from Old English hwēol, from Proto-West Germanic *hwehwl, from Proto-Germanic *hwehwlą, *hweulō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlóm, *kʷékʷlos, *kʷékʷléh₂, reduplication of *kʷel- (“to turn”) and a suffix (literally "(the thing that) turns and turns").
wheel.g: A circular device capable of rotating on its axis, facilitating movement or transportation or performing labour in machines.

wheelwork.g: An assembly of wheels serving a mechanical purpose.

whelp.e: From Middle English whelp, from Old English hwelp, from Proto-West Germanic *hwelp, from Proto-Germanic *hwelpaz (compare Dutch welp, German Welpe, Welfe, Old Norse hvelpr, Norwegian Nynorsk kvelp, Danish hvalp), from pre-Germanic *kʷelbos, of uncertain origin.
whelp.g: A young offspring of a various carnivores (canid, ursid, felid, pinniped), especially of a dog or a wolf, the young of a bear or similar mam

whelp.e: From Middle English whelpen, from Old English hwelpian, derived from hwelp.

when.e: From Middle English when(ne), whan(ne), from Old English hwonne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwannē, from Proto-West Germanic *hwan, from Proto-Germanic *hwan (“at what time, when”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís (interrogative base). Interjection sense: a playful misunderstanding of "say when" (i.e.
when.g: At what time? At which time? Upon which occasion or circumstance? Used to introduce direct or indirect questions about time.

whence.e: From Middle English whennes, from Old English hwanon (with adverbial genitive -s), related to hwonne (whence when). Analyzable as when + -s.
whence.g: From where, from which: from which place or source.

whenever.e: From Middle English whan evere, whanne ever, whanne evere, whener, when ever; equivalent to when + -ever.

whensoever.e: From Middle English quen-so-ever, wensoever, whanne so evere, whan-so-ever, whan-so-evere, whenne-soever, when so evyr. By surface analysis, when + so + ever.
whensoever.g: whenever; at any time at all

where.e: From Middle English wher, from Old English hwǣr (“where”, literally “at what place”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwār, from Proto-Germanic *hwar (“where”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷ- (interrogative pronoun).
where.g: In, at or to what place.

whereas.e: From where + as (“that”); first attested in the meaning of "where" in the 14th century.

whereby.g: By what, in which direction; how.

wherefore.e: From Middle English wherfor, wherfore, hwarfore, equivalent to where- (“what”) + for.
wherefore.g: Why, for what reason, because of what.

wherein.e: From Middle English wherin; equivalent to where- + in.

whereof.e: From Middle English wherof; equivalent to where + of.

whereon.e: From Middle English wheron, from wher + on. Equivalent to where + on.

wheresoever.e: From Middle English hwer se eaver, hwer-se-eaver, hwer so ever, qheresoevere, quar-sua-ever, quere-so-ever, wer so ever, wharsoever, where-sere, wheresoever, where so evere, wher ser, wher-sever, wher-so-ever, wher so evere, wher-so-evere, whe so er, whor so ever. By surface analysis, where + so + -ever.

whereto.e: From Middle English wherto, equivalent to where + to.
whereto.g: To what; to which place, whither?

whereunto.g: Unto what or which; to what purpose.

whereupon.e: From Middle English wherupon; equivalent to where- + upon.
whereupon.g: After which; in consequence; at which point.

wherewith.e: From Middle English wherwith. By surface analysis, where + with.

whet.e: Verb sense 1.3.3 (“to inculcate or teach (habits, information, etc.)”) is from Deuteronomy 6:6–7 in the Bible (New International Version): “These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children.” The word translated as impress is Hebrew שָׁנַן (shanán, “to be sharp; to sharpen, whet”).
whet.g: To sharpen (something, such as a knife or sword) by rubbing on an object, especially a whetstone; to hone.

whether.e: From Middle English whether, whather, from Old English hweþer, hwæþer, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaþar, from Proto-Germanic *hwaþeraz, comparative form of *hwaz (“who”).
whether.g: Introduces a simple indirect question (with no correlative).

whichever.e: From whiche ever, whiche evere, which ever, which evere; equivalent to which + -ever.

while.e: From Middle English whyle, from Old English hwīl, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīlu, from Proto-Germanic *hwīlō (compare Dutch wijl, Low German Wiel, German Weile, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål hvile (“rest”), Norwegian Nynorsk kvila (“rest”), Swedish vila (“rest”), Faroese and Icelandic hvíla (“rest”)) from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”).
while.g: An uncertain duration of time, a period of time.

whilst.e: From Late Middle English whilst, whilest, qwhilste (Northern England), quilest (Northwest Midlands), from whiles (“during the time that, while; only so long as; provided that; because, since; until”) + -t (excrescent suffix, perhaps due to a combination of -(e)s and the following word the, or influenced by the superlative suffix -est).
whilst.g: Often preceded by the: During the time; meanwhile.

whim.g: A fanciful impulse, or sudden change of idea.

whip.e: From Middle English whippen, wippen (“to flap violently”), from Middle Dutch wippen (“to swing, leap, dance, oscillate”) and Middle Low German wippen (“to move quickly”), from Proto-Germanic *wippōną (“to move back and forth”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyp- (“to shake; to swing”). (See Swedish vippa and Danish vippe (“to shake”)).
whip.g: A lash; a pliant, flexible instrument, such as a rod (commonly of cane or rattan) or a plaited or braided rope or thong (commonly of leather

whirl.e: From Middle English whirlen, contracted from earlier *whirvelen, *whervelen, possibly from Old English *hwyrflian, *hweorflian (attested in hwirflung, hwerflung (“change, vicissitude”)), frequentative form of Old English hweorfan (“to turn”), itself from Proto-West Germanic *hwerban, from Proto-Germanic *hwerbaną (“to turn”).
whirl.g: To rotate, revolve, spin or turn rapidly.

whirl.e: From Middle English whirl, wherwille, whorwhil, wervel, from Old English hwirfel, hwyrfel (“whirlpool”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwirbil, from Proto-Germanic *hwirbilaz, *hwarbilaz (“swirl, whirl, whirlpool”), equivalent to wharve + -el.

whirlwind.e: From Middle English whirlewind, whirlewynde, equivalent to whirl + wind.
whirlwind.g: A windstorm of limited extent, such as a tornado, dust devil, or waterspout, characterized by an inward spiral motion of the air with an upw

whisper.e: From Middle English whisperen, from Old English hwisprian (“to mutter, murmur, whisper”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwisprōn, from Proto-Germanic *hwisprōną (“to hiss, whistle, whisper”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweys-, *ḱwey- (“to hiss, whistle, whisper”).
whisper.g: The act of speaking in a quiet voice, especially without vibration of the vocal cords; the sound thus produced.

whisperer.e: From whisper + -er. The extended senses were popularized by the film The Horse Whisperer (1998).

whistle.e: From Middle English whistel, whistil, whistle, from Old English hwistle, from the verb (see below).
whistle.g: A device designed to be placed in the mouth and blown, or driven by steam or some other mechanism, to make a whistling sound.

whistle.e: From Middle English whistlen, from Old English hwistlan, hwistlian (“to whistle”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwistlōn, from Proto-Germanic *hwistlōną (“to make a hissing sound”).
whistle.g: To make a shrill, high-pitched sound by forcing air through the mouth. To produce a whistling sound, restrictions to the flow of air are cre

whistling.e: From Middle English whistlynge, equivalent to whistle + -ing.

whit.e: From Middle English wiȝt, wight, from Old English wiht (“wight, person, creature, being, whit, thing, something, anything”), from Proto-Germanic *wihtą (“thing, creature”) or *wihtiz (“essence, object”), from Proto-Indo-European *wekti- (“cause, sake, thing”), from *wekʷ- (“to say, tell”).
whit.g: The smallest part or particle imaginable; an iota.

white.e: From Middle English whit, hwit, from Old English hwīt, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīt, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweydós, a byform of *ḱweytós (“bright; shine”).
white.g: Bright and colourless; reflecting equal quantities of all frequencies of visible light.

whitewash.e: Noun sense 5.1 (“medicinal preparation for treating skin diseases”) is a calque of New Latin lōtiō alba (literally “white wash”).
whitewash.g: A mixture of a powdered mineral substance (often slaked lime (containing calcium hydroxide), chalk (calcium carbonate), or both) and water w

whither.e: From Middle English whider (“to what place?; into or to which; to what place, where; no matter where, to wherever”), from Old English hwider, hwæder (“to what place, where”), from Proto-Germanic *hwadrê (“to what place, where”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷos (“what; which”), from *kʷ- (the primary interrogative root).

whithersoever.e: From Middle English whidersoevere. By surface analysis, whither + so + -ever.

whoever.e: From Middle English whoever. By surface analysis, who + -ever.
whoever.g: Who ever: an emphatic form of who.

whole.e: From Middle English whol, hol, hole (“healthy, unhurt, whole”), from Old English hāl (“healthy, safe”), from Proto-West Germanic *hail, from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“whole, safe, sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos (“healthy, whole”). The spelling with wh-, attested since ca.

wholehearted.e: From whole + hearted. First appears before 1628 in the publications of John Preston, a clergyman in the Church of England.
wholehearted.g: Showing enthusiastic and unconditional commitment; having no reservations.

wholeheartedly.g: In a wholehearted (“showing enthusiastic and unconditional commitment”) manner; without reserve; enthusiastically, unreservedly.

wholesome.e: From earlier holesome, from Middle English holsom, holsum, helsum, halsum, from Old English *hālsum, *hǣlsum, from Proto-West Germanic *hailasam, from Proto-Germanic *hailasamaz, equivalent to whole + -some or hale (“healthy”) + -some.
wholesome.g: Promoting good physical health and well-being.

wholly.e: From Middle English holly (“wholly”), holeliche, holliche (also as halely, hallich, etc.). By surface analysis, whol(e) + -ly.
wholly.g: Completely and entirely; to the fullest extent.

whomever.e: From Middle English whomever; equivalent to whom + -ever.
whomever.g: Whatever person or persons (as object of verb or preposition).

whomsoever.e: From Middle English whom so evere, whom soever, whom-so-ever, whom-so-evere, whomsoever, whom-so-evyr. By surface analysis, whom + so + -ever.
whomsoever.g: Whatever person or persons (as object of a verb or preposition): emphasised or elaborated form of whomever.

whore.e: From Middle English hore, from Old English hōre, from Proto-Germanic *hōrǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros (“loved”), from *keh₂- (“to wish; desire”).
whore.g: Synonym of prostitute: a person (especially a woman) who offers sexual services for payment.

whoredom.e: From Middle English horedom, hordom, from Old Norse hórdómr, ultimately corresponding to whore + -dom.
whoredom.g: The state of being a whore, prostitution; sexual indulgence, fornication.

whoso.e: From Middle English hoe so, hoo so, hoo-so, from Old English hwā swā; equivalent to who + so.

whosoever.e: From Middle English whosoever. By surface analysis, who + so + -ever.
whosoever.g: Whatever person or persons: emphasised or elaborated form of whoever.

why.e: From Middle English why, from Old English hwȳ (“why”), from Proto-Germanic *hwī (“by what, how”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷey, instrumental case of *kʷís (“who”), *kʷid (“what”).
why.g: For what cause, reason, or purpose.
